reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of purine catabolism causing a block in the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid

Type I results from isolated xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase deficiency (XDH), while type II results from molybdenum cofactor sulfurase (MOCOS) deficiency affecting both xanthine oxidase and aldehyde oxidase
The biochemical hallmark is very low or undetectable serum and urinary uric acid (hypouricaemia) with markedly increased urinary xanthine and hypoxanthine
Poorly soluble xanthine can precipitate to form radiolucent urinary calculi, causing renal colic, haematuria, urinary tract infection and occasionally acute kidney injury
Many individuals are asymptomatic and detected incidentally through unexplained hypouricaemia on routine biochemistry
Xanthine can also deposit in muscle, rarely causing myopathy with pain and cramps

Management is largely conservative with high fluid intake, a purine-restricted diet and, in some, urinary alkalinisation to reduce xanthine stone formation; allopurinol is ineffective and inappropriate
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary xanthinuria is an inborn error of the terminal steps of purine degradation. Xanthine oxidase/dehydrogenase normally oxidises hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid; when it is deficient (type I) or when the molybdenum cofactor sulfurase needed for its activity is lacking (type II, which also disables aldehyde oxidase), these purines cannot be converted to uric acid. Consequently uric acid levels are strikingly low while xanthine and hypoxanthine accumulate and are excreted in excess. Because xanthine is far less soluble than uric acid, it may crystallise in the urinary tract to form calculi and can deposit in tissues such as muscle.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of hypouricaemia (renal hypouricaemia, Fanconi syndrome, drugs)
Iatrogenic xanthinuria from xanthine oxidase inhibitor therapy
Molybdenum cofactor deficiency (severe neonatal encephalopathy with sulfite involvement)
Other radiolucent stone-forming conditions such as uric acid or 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stones
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency for disordered purine handling
additionalInvestigations: Serum and urinary uric acid (characteristically very low)
Renal tract ultrasound or low-dose imaging for radiolucent calculi
Enzyme assay or allopurinol loading test to distinguish type I from type II
Molecular genetic testing of XDH and MOCOS genes
redFlags: Obstructing xanthine stones causing acute kidney injury
Recurrent urinary tract infection with obstructing calculi
Progressive renal impairment from recurrent stone disease
Myopathy with rising creatine kinase from tissue xanthine deposition
reference.prognosis: Many patients remain asymptomatic with a normal life expectancy; in those who form stones, adequate hydration and dietary measures usually limit complications, though recurrent obstructive calculi can occasionally threaten renal function.
pitfalls: Prescribing a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, which cannot work and worsens xanthine load
Overlooking radiolucent xanthine stones on plain imaging
Dismissing marked hypouricaemia as laboratory error rather than investigating it
Failing to distinguish type I from type II, which has implications for associated aldehyde oxidase deficiency
Not advising adequate fluid intake to prevent stone formation
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
